We have mass spectrum data: peaks at m/z 268.1939 (intensity 100), 269.1971 (20.5), 270.2003 (1.99), 271.2034 (0.122), 272.20655 (0.0053), 273.20964 (0.00017), 274.21408 (tiny). This looks like isotopic pattern of a molecule containing chlorine? Chlorine isotopes: 35Cl (75.78% at M), 37Cl (24.22%) gives M+2 about 1/3 intensity. Here M+1 is 20% of base, M+2 is ~2% of base, M+3 ~0.12% etc. That pattern resembles presence of sulfur? Sulfur isotopes: 32S (95.02%), 33S (0.75%), 34S (4.21%), 36S (0.02%). That gives M+2 about 4% of base, M+1 about 0.75% of base. Not matching. Chlorine gives M+2 ~1/3 of base (approx 0.33). Here M+2 is 0.02 (2%) not 33%. So not chlorine. Bromine isotopes: 79Br (50.69%), 81Br (49.31%) gives M+2 ~ similar intensity to M. Not matching. Iodine only one isotope. So maybe carbon isotopic pattern: 13C ~1.1% per carbon. If many carbons, M+1 intensity grows. The pattern shows M+1 ~20% of base, M+2 ~2% of base, M+3 ~0.12% etc. This suggests roughly 18 carbons? Because 13C natural abundance 1.1% per carbon, M+1 intensity ~ n*1.1% = 20% => n≈18. So carbon is present. Also hydrogen 2H (D) 0.015% negligible. Nitrogen 15N 0.37% per N, contributes to M+1. Oxygen 17O 0.038% per O, 18O 0.2% contributes to M+2. Sulfur isotopes produce M+2 ~4% per S. The observed M+2 is 2% of base, could be due to combination of 13C+13C (two 13C) or 34S etc. But we need elements that can be definitively identified from isotope distribution patterns visible. Which elements have distinctive patterns? Chlorine, bromine, sulfur have characteristic patterns. Here pattern does not match chlorine or bromine. Sulfur pattern would give M+2 ~4% of base, but we have 2% (maybe less). Could be presence of one S? If one S, M+2 ~4% of base, but we see 2% (maybe due to overlapping contributions). Might not be definitive.

We can retrieve isotopic distribution to compare.
